details:
**Eternal punishment of hunger and thirst**
Tantalus is punished in Tartarus by standing in a pool of water beneath fruit-laden branches. Whenever he bends to drink, the water recedes, and whenever he reaches for the fruit, the branches move out of reach. This punishment gives English the word "tantalize."

**Serving Pelops to the gods**
Tantalus killed his son Pelops, cooked him, and served him at a banquet to test whether the gods were truly all-knowing. The gods recognized the meal and refused it, and they restored Pelops to life.

**Pelops's ivory shoulder**
Demeter, distracted by grief over her lost daughter Persephone, absent-mindedly ate Pelops's shoulder at the banquet. When the gods brought Pelops back to life, they replaced the missing shoulder with one made of ivory.

**Stealing nectar and ambrosia**
Tantalus, a favorite of the gods, was invited to dine with them on Olympus. He stole their nectar and ambrosia to share with mortals, and in some versions he also revealed the gods' secrets to humans.

**Niobe**
The daughter of Tantalus, who boasted that her fourteen children made her superior to Leto, who had only two. Leto's children Apollo and Artemis killed all of Niobe's children, and the grieving Niobe was turned into a weeping rock on Mount Sipylus.

**Pelops's chariot race against Oenomaus**
Pelops, son of Tantalus, won the hand of Hippodamia by defeating her father, King Oenomaus, in a chariot race. He won by bribing Oenomaus's charioteer Myrtilus to sabotage his master's chariot, then killed Myrtilus, bringing a curse on his descendants, the house of Atreus.

**King of Mount Sipylus (Lydia)**
Tantalus ruled from Mount Sipylus in Lydia (or Phrygia) in Asia Minor. In some accounts he was killed when a boulder from Mount Sipylus fell on him.

**Pandareus and the golden dog**
Pandareus stole a golden dog, which had guarded the infant Zeus on Crete, and gave it to Tantalus to keep. When Tantalus swore falsely to Hermes that he did not have the dog, he was punished, in some versions by being buried under Mount Sipylus.

**Son of Zeus and Plouto**
Tantalus was the son of Zeus and the nymph Plouto, who in some accounts was the daughter of Himas. This divine parentage explains why he was invited to dine with the gods.

**Broteas**
Another son of Tantalus, a hunter and sculptor who was considered ugly. He was said to have carved the oldest image of the mother goddess on Mount Sipylus.

**Tantalus, first husband of Clytemnestra**
A grandson or descendant of the original Tantalus who shared his name. He was Clytemnestra's first husband until Agamemnon killed him and their infant child and took Clytemnestra as his own wife.
